A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work and provide readable text, mathematics, diagrams, and algorithms. V1's Appendices A, B, and C correspond to v2's Sections 10, 11, and 9.3, respectively; their relocation does not represent missing material.

before.justification: V1 presents algorithms, sample-complexity guarantees, and proofs, including its appendices, but no original experimental, simulation, or data-analysis outcomes.

after.justification: V2 remains theoretical. Its new maximum-likelihood section describes an algorithmic approach and guarantees, without reporting an executed experiment or empirical outcomes.

M1.justification: V1 constructs experts through clipping and bucketing conditional probabilities, then samples both structures and conditional distributions. V2 instead estimates one add-one distribution per DAG using a separate sample batch, substantially changing expert construction and subsequent sampling. Section 12 also introduces a maximum-likelihood adaptation of the dynamic programs.

E1.justification: Neither version uses datasets or executes evaluation tasks. Trees, chordal graphs, and bounded-vertex-cover graphs are theoretical learning classes, not experimentally evaluated coverage.

E2.justification: Neither version experimentally evaluates comparison methods. V2's new Table 2 compares guarantees and assumptions of prior work; it is not a baseline experiment.

E3.justification: Neither version reports an experimental evaluation protocol. Revised sample allocations and algorithm parameters concern the proposed learning procedures and theoretical guarantees.

E4.justification: Neither version contains empirical ablations, sensitivity tests, robustness experiments, or case studies. The contamination discussion and supplementary proofs are theoretical.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated experimental runs, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. PAC success probabilities and concentration arguments are theoretical guarantees, not experimental uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Neither PDF reports measured performance, experimental runtimes, or empirical qualitative findings. Changes to sample-complexity bounds and approximation factors are formal results assessed under T1.

T1.justification: V1's clipping/bucketing cover analysis is replaced by a uniform add-one estimation guarantee in Theorem 7.8. For fixed d, proper agnostic complexity changes from ~O(n^3 k^(d+1)/(ε^2 δ^2)) in v1 Theorem 3.13 to ~O(n^3/(ε^2 δ^2) + nk^(d+1)/ε) in v2 Theorem 7.12. Improper, tree, and vertex-cover bounds also change. The semi-agnostic approximation factor becomes 4 instead of 3. Section 12 adds MLE reasoning; the former lower-bound appendix is retained.

C1.justification: V2's main chordal theorem explicitly claims polynomial dependence on alphabet size k for fixed indegree, extending v1's fixed-k technical guarantees. Its headline tree theorem changes from an agnostic (ε,3)-approximation to realizable learning. Semi-agnostic learning remains in the detailed results with factor 4, although the new conclusion inconsistently retains factor 3.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive qualifications about obtaining the required known skeleton, explains the dependence on indegree, and distinguishes MLE's proper-learning guarantees from EWA's realizable improper-learning advantage. It also explicitly limits the contamination comparison to cases with small KL contamination. These refine applicability and interpretation within the existing framework.

D1.justification: V2 specifies the preliminary sample batch and passes it explicitly through revised chordal-learning pseudocode. Remark 2.3 and Section 9.3 add operation counts and sample-pass details for computing conditional distributions and edge weights. Neither version supplies an executable implementation or empirical resource information.

R1.justification: V1 claims that learning high-dimensional distributions through online learning had not been reported previously. V2 Section 4 acknowledges earlier approaches by Catoni, Yang, and van der Hoeven et al., positioning its contribution around computational efficiency for structured distributions. Additional KL-learning, density-estimation, and MLE literature substantially expands and corrects the research positioning.

P1.justification: V2 rewrites the abstract and introductory narrative, promotes results, techniques, related work, and open problems into separate sections, and presents chordal learning before tree learning. It integrates the former appendices into the numbered body and adds a concluding Discussion section. This is substantial reorganization beyond renumbering.

P2.justification: New Tables 1 and 2 consolidate sample-complexity regimes and comparisons with prior work. V2 redisplays learning pseudocode in the techniques overview and reformats technical algorithm blocks. V1's vertically stacked chordal illustrations become a horizontal Figure 2 with a combined caption; Figure 1 retains its content but changes caption placement.

improvement.justification: The add-one construction and its analysis address an important restriction: v1's detailed sampler is efficient only for constant alphabet size, whereas v2 supports polynomial dependence on k and substantially tighter agnostic bounds. V2 also corrects its broad novelty claim. These gains outweigh the weaker approximation factor, although summary inconsistencies remain: Section 2 overstates the near-optimal agnostic guarantee, and Section 13 still claims factor 3 instead of the theorems' factor 4.
